Vision Transformer for Blood Cell Classification & Differential Counting¶

A portfolio project built to explore automated haematology analysis (miniaturised haematology analyser — VPT-based blood cell classification & differential counting)

This notebook builds, trains, and clinically benchmarks a Vision Transformer (ViT) that classifies individual blood cells from microscopy images and aggregates those per-cell predictions into a per-image differential count — then validates that count against ground truth the way you would validate a new analyser against a reference/commercial one (Bland-Altman agreement, bias, limits of agreement).

Pipeline: microscopy image → cell detection/crop → ViT classification → per-image differential count → statistical benchmarking against reference counts.

This mirrors, at small scale, the exact workflow described in the job posting:

"develop and fine-tune a Vision Pre-trained Transformer (VPT) model for the classification and differential counting of blood cells... benchmarked against established commercial haematology analysers using appropriate statistical and machine-learning performance measures."

Scope & honesty about limitations¶

This was built in a sandboxed environment with no access to the Hugging Face Hub or Kaggle (only PyPI and GitHub were reachable), so two simplifications were necessary and are called out explicitly rather than hidden:

  1. Dataset: uses the public 364-image BCCD (Blood Cell Count and Detection) dataset, which labels three classes (RBC / WBC / Platelets) rather than the full 5-part WBC differential (neutrophil / lymphocyte / monocyte / eosinophil / basophil). The code and methodology generalise directly to a proper WBC differential dataset (e.g. the Barcelona PBC dataset, Raabin-WBC, or in-house miniaturised-analyser images) — see the "Next steps" section at the end.
  2. Weights: trains a ViT from a random initialisation rather than fine-tuning a Hub checkpoint, since the checkpoint download was not reachable from this environment. model.py is written so that switching to a real pretrained checkpoint (e.g. google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k) is a one-line change (build_model(pretrained=True)) once Hub access is available.

Everything else — the ViT architecture, training loop, per-cell evaluation, and the count-agreement benchmarking methodology — is exactly what would be used in production.

2. Data: from whole microscopy fields to labeled single-cell crops¶

The BCCD dataset provides 364 microscopy fields, each with Pascal-VOC bounding box annotations for every red blood cell (RBC), white blood cell (WBC), and platelet in the field (data_prep.py). Each bounding box is cropped out (with 12% padding for context) into its own labeled image — turning an object detection dataset into a cell classification dataset, and giving us per-image ground-truth counts to benchmark against later.

Images (not crops) are split 70/15/15 into train/val/test, so cells from the same microscopy field never leak across splits.

In [2]:
train_ds = CellCropDataset("train")
val_ds = CellCropDataset("val")
test_ds = CellCropDataset("test")

for name, ds in [("train", train_ds), ("val", val_ds), ("test", test_ds)]:
    print(f"{name:5s}: {len(ds):5d} crops  {ds.class_counts()}")

Example cropped cells, by class:

In [3]:
display(IPImage(filename=str(RESULTS_DIR / "sample_crops.png")))

Note the heavy class imbalance — RBCs vastly outnumber WBCs and platelets, exactly as in a real blood smear. Training uses class-weighted cross-entropy to compensate (train.py::compute_class_weights).

3. Model: Vision Transformer¶

model.py builds a transformers.ViTForImageClassification — a standard ViT: image → non-overlapping patches → linear patch embedding → learned position embeddings → a stack of pre-norm transformer encoder blocks (multi-head self-attention + MLP) → a [CLS] token pooled through a linear classification head.

For CPU training within this environment, the config is scaled down from vit-base (86M params) to a small variant (~2.7M params, 6 layers, hidden size 192, 96x96 images, 8x8 patches) — same architecture family, sized to train in minutes rather than requiring a GPU cluster.

In [4]:
model = build_model(pretrained=False)
print(f"Model parameters: {count_params(model):,}")

4. Training¶

Trained for 10 epochs with AdamW, cosine LR decay, and class-weighted cross-entropy loss. (train.py; re-run with python train.py --epochs 10 — took ~17 minutes on 2 CPU cores.)

5. Held-out test set: classification performance¶

(evaluate.py) Loads the best checkpoint and evaluates on the test-split crops (cells from microscopy fields the model never saw during training).

In [7]:
with open(RESULTS_DIR / "evaluation_results.json") as f:
    eval_results = json.load(f)

print(f"Test accuracy: {eval_results['test_accuracy']:.4f}\n")
report = eval_results["classification_report"]
for cls in CLASSES:
    r = report[cls]
    print(f"{cls:10s} precision {r['precision']:.3f}  recall {r['recall']:.3f}  "
          f"f1 {r['f1-score']:.3f}  support {int(r['support'])}")
print(f"\nMacro F1: {report['macro avg']['f1-score']:.3f}")

6. Clinical-style benchmarking: differential count agreement¶

This is the step that most directly mirrors the job description: per-cell predictions are aggregated back into a per-microscopy-image differential count (RBC / WBC / Platelet counts per field), then compared against the ground-truth (annotated) counts for that same field — exactly how you'd validate a new analyser's differential count against a reference method.

Two views:

  • Scatter plot of predicted vs. reference count per image, with Pearson r.
  • Bland-Altman plot of agreement (mean vs. difference), which is the standard method-comparison tool in clinical chemistry/haematology — it reports bias (systematic over/under-counting) and 95% limits of agreement, and is far more informative than a single correlation coefficient (see note below).
In [9]:
display(IPImage(filename=str(RESULTS_DIR / "count_scatter.png")))
In [10]:
display(IPImage(filename=str(RESULTS_DIR / "bland_altman.png")))

Reading the benchmarking results¶

  • RBC: essentially perfect count agreement (r = 1.000, bias = 0.00) — expected, since RBC classification itself was perfect (100% recall).
  • Platelets: strong agreement (r = 0.945, bias = -0.05, tight limits of agreement) — a few images are off by 1-2 cells, consistent with the ~91% crop-level recall.
  • WBC: crop-level classification is strong (96.4% recall, 91.5% precision), but the per-image count Pearson r is misleadingly low (0.238). This is a real, well-known pitfall in method-comparison statistics, not a modelling bug: WBC-per-field counts in this dataset have very little spread (mostly 0-2 per field), so Pearson r is unstable and uninformative at low, narrow-range counts — a couple of off-by-one images dominate the correlation even though the absolute agreement is good (bias = 0.05 cells, 95% limits of agreement = [-0.73, 0.84] cells). This is precisely why Bland-Altman (bias + limits of agreement), not correlation alone, is the appropriate statistic for validating a differential count against a reference method — and why the JD's phrase "appropriate statistical and machine-learning performance measures" matters: the right metric depends on the count distribution, not just habit.

7. Limitations & path to a production version¶

What's demonstrated here at small scale, and how it would scale up for a production deployment:

This project Production version for the role
3 classes (RBC/WBC/Platelets) from BCCD Full 5-part WBC differential (neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, basophil), trained on a proper differential dataset (e.g. Barcelona PBC dataset, Raabin-WBC) or in-house labelled data from the miniaturised analyser
ViT trained from random init (~2.7M params) Fine-tune a Hub-pretrained ViT (e.g. google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k) — model.py already supports this via pretrained=True
364 microscopy fields, single imaging system Curate/harmonise images across the commercial and miniaturised imaging systems named in the JD, explicitly testing cross-device generalisability
Bounding-box crops as a proxy for "detection" A dedicated cell-detection stage (or an end-to-end detection+classification model) feeding the ViT classifier
Bland-Altman + Pearson r on synthetic/public ground truth Same statistical framework, benchmarked against a real commercial haematology analyser's reported differential counts

The engineering (data pipeline with strict image-level train/val/test splitting to avoid leakage, class-weighted training, checkpointing, per-class metrics, and clinical-style agreement statistics) is written to scale directly to that production setting.
